title: The flute the gopis could only hear
hookLine: the gopis can only hear Krishna's flute from the village, and the whole forest stops to listen
carry: hearing about God is already bhakti
tomorrow: why would the gopis be jealous of a piece of bamboo?

cards: A calf is drinking from its mother, and it stops. The milk is still in its mouth. It doesn't swallow.
It just stands there, ears up. Somewhere past the pasture, among the trees, someone is playing a flute.

That calf comes from the Bhagavata Purana, from a chapter where the women of Vraja, the gopis, stay behind in the village while Krishna takes the cows to the forest. They can't see him. They can only hear him.
So they tell each other what the sound is doing to everything it reaches.

teach.h: HE WALKS INTO THE AUTUMN FOREST.
teach.b: In this chapter Krishna doesn't teach anyone. He just plays, walking into the autumn forest with his brother Balarama and the herd.
The gopis fill in the picture from memory: a peacock feather in his hair, a yellow cloth, a garland of forest flowers, his lips on the bamboo. Then they turn to the listeners.
The cows lift their ears and drink in the sound; the calves stand with milk in their mouths. The birds settle on the branches and close their eyes.
The rivers, the gopis say, slow their current and reach out with their waves to hold his feet. Even the clouds drift over him to give him shade.
Not priests, not kings: cows, birds, water, weather.

teach.h: THE GOPIS HEAR, BUT CAN'T SEE.
teach.b: And the gopis themselves? At home, at their work. They can't see him.
They can only hear him, and tell each other about him, and that is enough to fill them. Hindus take this very seriously.

Later in the same Bhagavata, the boy Prahlada names nine ways of bhakti, loving devotion to God, and the first two are hearing about him and singing about him. The gopis are doing both, from their kitchens.
That's why Hindus gather for katha, where a teller reads and explains the Bhagavata for days, sometimes a whole week, and for kirtan, singing God's names together. Nobody in the room sees Krishna.
They listen, like a calf that forgot to swallow.

how: Hindus gather to hear the Bhagavata told aloud in katha, often over seven days (a Bhagavata saptah), and to sing God's names in kirtan; the chapter on the flute is read and sung in devotion, and temple images show Krishna holding his flute.

s: the gopis follow Krishna into the forest to hear him play
in this chapter they stay in the village and describe the music to each other.
the calves stop drinking with milk still in their mouths
the gopis say the calves stand still, listening, and don't swallow.
in the Bhagavata, just hearing about God counts as devotion
Prahlada's nine ways of bhakti begin with hearing about God and singing about him.

games.q: you're at a katha. for three hours a teller reads the Bhagavata and everyone just listens. by the gopis' story, what's happening?
o: nothing yet. real devotion starts when you see God.
the listening is the worship: hearing about Krishna is bhakti.
it's polite waiting. the real worship is the aarti at the end.
games.why: the gopis never saw him play. they heard, and told each other, and that was their devotion. Prahlada's nine ways of bhakti start with hearing.

practice: Be one of the listeners in the forest. Let your eyes close or soften, and let sounds come to you, the room, the street, your own breath, without naming them. If a sound pulls you into thinking, come back with the next one.
If you pray, softly hum one of Krishna's names, Gopala or Govinda, and listen to it as if it were the flute calling. If you don't, let one sound stand for something you love, and just listen.

wordCard.voice: The flute. Krishna's bamboo flute, whose music, the gopis say, stops cows, birds, deer, rivers and clouds in the forest of Vraja.

orig.note: Sanskrit: bamboo, a flute. Tradition calls this chapter the Venu Gita, the song of the flute.
